items.title: Sine & Cosine Rules, Area of a Triangle

moments.title: Beyond right triangles
moments.text: The presenter introduces the sine rule, cosine rule and area formula.

moments.title: Pair opposite sides and angles

moments.text: A known angle and its opposite side form a useful pair.

moments.text: Set up an equation involving the $30^\circ$ and $100^\circ$ angles and their opposite sides.

moments.text: Substitute sides $40$ and $50$ and the included angle $30^\circ$ into the cosine rule.

moments.text: Use all three sides and place the square of the side opposite the requested angle in the subtraction.

moments.text: The diagram uses adjacent sides $50$ and $45$; the written denominator uses $40$ instead of $45$.

moments.title: Area from two sides and included angle

notes.title: Correct the cosine-rule denominator
notes.text: Around 8:34, the diagram has sides $50$, $45$ and $30$ cm. The angle is opposite $30$ cm, but the written denominator uses $2(50)(40)$.

notes.title: A formula beyond non-right triangles
notes.text: The sine rule, cosine rule and $\frac12ab\sin C$ also apply to right triangles. For $C=90^\circ$ the cosine rule becomes Pythagoras’ theorem.

ican.text: I can label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides relative to a chosen acute angle.
I can use sine, cosine or tangent to find an unknown side or angle in a right triangle.
I can choose and apply the sine or cosine rule when the given measurements support it.
I can find a triangle’s area using two sides and their included angle.
I can check angle mode, opposite side–angle pairs, units and the reasonableness of an answer.

ku.text: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Relative to an acute angle $\theta$, the opposite side lies across from it and the adjacent side touches it but is not the hypotenuse.

The ratios are $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ and $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$. Choose the ratio containing the known side and the unknown side.

To find an acute angle, form a ratio and apply the appropriate inverse function. For example, $\cos\theta=5/8$ gives $\theta=\cos^{-1}(5/8)\approx51.3^\circ$ in degree mode. Inverse cosine here is a function, not a reciprocal.

In triangle $ABC$, side $a$ is opposite angle $A$, and similarly for $b,B$ and $c,C$. Label the diagram before applying a rule. All angles in a non-degenerate triangle are positive and sum to $180^\circ$.

Use the sine rule $\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}$ when a complete opposite side–angle pair and another relevant measurement are known. Choose the two fractions that contain the known values and the desired unknown.

Use the cosine rule $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$ to find a side when two sides and their included angle are known. When all three sides are known, rearrange to $\cos C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$ to find the angle opposite $c$.

For two sides $a,b$ and their included angle $C$, the area is $K=\frac12ab\sin C$. This follows from $K=\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{perpendicular height}$, because the height relative to base $a$ is $b\sin C$.

Check triangle feasibility: positive side lengths must satisfy the triangle inequalities, and a calculated sine or cosine of a real angle must lie between $-1$ and $1$. Interpret answers in the context, with length or square units as appropriate.
The local AI syllabus guidance excludes the ambiguous case of the sine rule from SL 3.2. The rules above still require matching opposite sides and angles correctly.

terms.text: The angle formed where the two specified sides meet.
An angle and the side directly across from it, such as $A$ and $a$.
A function used to find an angle from a trigonometric ratio. Use the angle unit requested.
The distance from a vertex to the line containing the chosen base, measured at a right angle.

formula.text: Right triangle: $\sin\theta=O/H$, $\cos\theta=A/H$ and $\tan\theta=O/A$, where $O,A,H$ are the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse lengths relative to $\theta$.
Sine rule: $\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}$, with each side opposite its matching capital-letter angle.
Area: $K=\frac12ab\sin C$, where $C$ is included between sides $a$ and $b$.

worked.prompt: A triangular garden has vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$, with $AB=10$ m, $AC=7$ m and included angle $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the side $AB$.

parts.label: a
parts.a: In right triangle $ACD$, $AC=7$ is the hypotenuse. Thus $AD=7\cos60^\circ=3.5$ m and $CD=7\sin60^\circ=\frac{7\sqrt3}{2}$ m $\approx6.06$ m. Since $0<AD<10$, $D$ lies on segment $AB$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the length of $BC$ exactly and to three significant figures.
parts.a: Using the cosine rule with included angle $A$: $BC^2=10^2+7^2-2(10)(7)\cos60^\circ=79$. Hence $BC=\sqrt{79}$ m $\approx8.89$ m. As a check, $DB=10-3.5=6.5$ and $BC^2=DB^2+CD^2=79$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find the area of the garden.
parts.a: $K=\frac12(10)(7)\sin60^\circ$. This gives $K=\frac{35\sqrt3}{2}\text{ m}^2\approx30.3\text{ m}^2$. Equivalently, use base $AB$ and height $CD$ from part (a).

parts.label: d
parts.q: Find the size of angle $ABC$. Explain why your result is reasonable.
parts.a: In right triangle $BCD$, $\tan B=CD/DB=\frac{7\sqrt3}{13}$, so $B=\tan^{-1}(7\sqrt3/13)\approx43.0^\circ$. The remaining angle is approximately $77.0^\circ$, and $B$ is opposite the shortest side, $AC=7$ m, so $B$ should be the smallest angle.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Use the sine rule to calculate $BC$ from angles $A$ and $B$ and compare with part (b).
parts.a: First, $C=180^\circ-60^\circ-B\approx76.9961^\circ$. Match opposite pairs: $BC/\sin60^\circ=7/\sin B$. Therefore $BC=7\sin60^\circ/\sin B\approx8.89$ m, consistent with part (b). Use the unrounded $B$ in the calculation.

kq.q: Why must the angle in the area formula be included between the two sides?
kq.model: Taking one side as a base, the other side and their included angle determine the perpendicular height. A different angle would need a different matching side for that height.

kq.q: Why does the cosine rule reduce to Pythagoras in a right triangle?
Why does inverse sine not mean divide by sine?
kq.model: Inverse sine reverses sine over its principal interval to return an angle from a ratio. A reciprocal instead divides $1$ by a numerical sine value.

kq.q: How can side lengths help check angles?
kq.model: In a triangle, the longer side is opposite the larger angle. If a result reverses this order, check the side–angle labels and calculations.
